Senior Music Editor at Screen Rant, Sarah's love of sound and story drive the beat. A globetrotting brand whisperer and award-winning journalist, she’s built cross-cultural narratives around the world—but music has always been her true north. She launched DJ Mag North America, successfully introducing the iconic UK brand to the U.S. market. Previously, she carved a space for EDM inside the pages of VIBE, blending electronic and hip-hop culture long before it was trendy.

The fastest way to convince someone they do not like Westerns may be to hand them a list of old classics and tell them they are important. Plenty of them are masterpieces, but that does not necessarily make them the easiest way into a genre that can already feel intimidating from the outside.

For a lot of modern viewers, Yellowstone has already done some of the work. Taylor Sheridan's hit series became a gateway drug to Western storytelling by proving that cowboys could feel completely contemporary. Anyone looking to dip their toes into Western film waters has myriad other friendly places to start. Westerns can be funny, fast, romantic, or structured like thrillers. They can also get surprisingly strange, particularly once filmmakers started taking apart the familiar rules in revisionist Western movies.

These six movies offer different ways into the genre without feeling like homework. Start with Billy Crystal learning how to survive a cattle drive, and before long, dusty frontier towns riddled with outlaws and cattle may not seem so intimidating after all.

City Slickers (1991)

City Slickers may be the perfect Western for someone who does not think they like Westerns because its main characters don't belong in one either. Billy Crystal plays Mitch Robbins, a New Yorker facing a midlife crisis who joins his friends on a cattle drive through the Southwest.

The comedy makes the cowboy setting approachable, but the movie never treats it as a joke.

The comedy makes the cowboy setting approachable, but the movie never treats it as a joke. Jack Palance's Oscar-winning Curly gives Mitch a glimpse of the harder philosophy underneath frontier life, while the cattle drive supplies enough danger to qualify as a genuine adventure. Viewers effectively learn how to appreciate the Western alongside Mitch.

Maverick (1994)

Maverick takes another easy route into the genre: it is essentially a con-artist comedy wearing cowboy boots. Mel Gibson plays gambler Bret Maverick, who needs to raise enough money to enter a high-stakes poker tournament while repeatedly crossing paths with Jodie Foster's equally slippery Annabelle Bransford.

Richard Donner never asks audiences to take the Western setting too seriously. The pleasure comes from watching the characters cheat, flirt, bluff, and talk their way out of trouble. James Garner's presence also connects the movie to the original Maverick TV series, giving newcomers a taste of classic Western history without turning the experience into a lesson.

The Quick And The Dead (1995)

Sam Raimi makes the Old West look like the setting for a comic book in The Quick and the Dead. Sharon Stone plays a mysterious gunslinger who enters a deadly quick-draw tournament run by Gene Hackman's ruthless John Herod, with a young Leonardo DiCaprio and Russell Crowe among the competitors.

That tournament structure makes the movie ridiculously easy to watch. Every new opponent brings another showdown, while Raimi uses the same visual energy he would later bring to Spider-Man. The movie has since been reconsidered as one of Sam Raimi's most underrated films, and its exaggerated style makes it a particularly good gateway for action fans.

Tombstone (1993)

By the time a beginner reaches Tombstone, they are getting much closer to the Western most people picture in their heads. There are lawmen, saloons, outlaw cowboys, and the Gunfight at the O.K. Corral, but none of it feels like dusty film history thanks to a stacked cast and an unusually quotable script.

Kurt Russell makes Wyatt Earp immediately accessible, but Val Kilmer's Doc Holliday is the reason many people fall in love with the movie. Even some of the things that make Tombstone harder to watch today have not diminished its reputation as one of the most entertaining modern Westerns. It is history turned into a crowd-pleaser.

3:10 To Yuma (2007)

Close

For viewers ready to leave the comedy behind, 3:10 to Yuma demonstrates just how tense a Western can be. Christian Bale plays struggling rancher Dan Evans, who agrees to help escort captured outlaw Ben Wade, played by Russell Crowe, to a train that will take him to prison.

James Mangold directs the story more like a pressure-cooker thriller than an old-fashioned cowboy epic. Wade's gang is closing in, Evans desperately needs the money, and neither man is quite what the other initially assumes. There is a reason 3:10 to Yuma belongs in any conversation about the most suspenseful Western movies.

True Grit (2010)

True Grit is where newcomers can graduate to something much closer to a traditional Western without having to jump back several decades. The Coen brothers tell the story through 14-year-old Mattie Ross, played brilliantly by Hailee Steinfeld, who hires U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn to hunt down the man who murdered her father.

True Grit is where newcomers can graduate to something much closer to a traditional Western...

Jeff Bridges' Cogburn has all the rough edges expected from an old Western lawman, but Mattie gives the movie a completely different center. Roger Deakins' cinematography makes the frontier beautiful without romanticizing its dangers. For anyone now ready to explore more great historical adventure movies, True Grit is an ideal bridge between modern filmmaking and the Western tradition that came before it.

True Grit, released in 2010, follows the determined journey of a 14-year-old girl seeking justice for her father's murder. She enlists U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn, known for his gritty resolve, to help capture the killer.
